args.body:
DEVIATION REPORT
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity — Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement
Counterparty Markup Analysis

Matter File 9 — Data Privacy Cybersecurity
Practice Area: Data Privacy & Cybersecurity
Deliverable: Full Deviation Report

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This deviation report compares the counterparty's latest markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against our firm's original draft and negotiation playbook, incorporating the transfer impact summary reflected in the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and within the controlling partner instructions received on this engagement.

The report reconciles each deviation introduced by the counterparty against: (a) the original draft of the agreement; (b) the firm's standard playbook positions for cross-border data transfer matters; (c) the disclosure schedules and exhibits that qualify the base materials; and (d) the partner instructions governing negotiation priorities. Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

II. SUMMARY OF COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS

The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions in our original draft. However, it introduces three significant deviations that must be evaluated, reconciled, and classified for negotiation:

  Deviation 1: Indemnification — Reduction of Cap and Conversion of Basket
      The indemnification cap is silently reduced from the firm-standard level.
      The loss basket is converted from a deductible structure to a tipping
      basket structure.

  Deviation 2: Material Adverse Effect — Addition of Regulatory Action Carve-Outs
      The definition of Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") adds carve-outs for
      regulatory action of precisely the kind at issue in this cross-border
      data transfer matter.

  Deviation 3: Survival Period — Reduction for Core Representations
      A new limitation period shortens the survival window for core
      representations below what Exhibit B of our original materials sets
      forth.

Each deviation is analyzed in detail below.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION: CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION

III.A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

Our original draft establishes an indemnification cap at the firm-standard level for a transaction of this nature involving cross-border data transfers. The standard playbook specifies a deductible-style basket, which requires the indemnified party to bear the first tranche of losses up to the basket threshold before any recovery is available. This structure is the firm's baseline for data privacy and cybersecurity matters, where regulatory exposure is meaningful and the client's overall risk allocation is calibrated around a deductible approach.

III.B. Counterparty Markup Change

The counterparty markup:
  (1) silently reduces the indemnification cap from the firm-standard level; and
  (2) converts the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket, meaning that once the basket threshold is surpassed, losses are recoverable from the first dollar rather than only the excess over the basket amount.

III.C. Transfer Impact Summary Reconciliation

The transfer impact summary, as informed by the disclosure schedules, identifies material retained liabilities relevant to this indemnification analysis. Specifically, Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the counterparty's indemnification changes would silently shift. These retained liabilities relate to cross-border data transfer exposures, including potential regulatory penalties, enforcement actions, and third-party claims arising from the data transfer operations. The markup's reduction of the indemnification cap and conversion to a tipping basket, taken together, alter the risk allocation in a manner that would shift a meaningful portion of these retained liabilities from the counterparty/incoming party to our client.

III.D. Partner Instruction

Under the controlling partner instruction (latest message in the deal team correspondence), the client will concede the basket conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket. This concession is directed and supersedes any earlier guidance reflecting a contrary or opposite priority ordering. Counsel should therefore not expend negotiating capital opposing the tipping-basket structure.

III.E. Deviation Assessment

  — Basket conversion: CONCEDED per partner instruction. No further negotiation
    required on this element.

  — Indemnification cap reduction: NOT addressed by the partner concession and
    remains a contested deviation. The cap reduction, in combination with the
    Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities, would materially shift risk to client.
    This deviation should be actively opposed. Because partner instructions
    only address the basket structure, the cap reduction remains a separate and
    unresolved point requiring a counterproposal restoring the firm-standard
    cap.

  Severity: HIGH (cap reduction remains active)
  Recommended action: Counterproposal to restore firm-standard cap; accept
  tipping-basket structure as instructed.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT: ADDITION OF REGULATORY ACTION CARVE-OUTS

IV.A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

The firm's original MAE definition follows established precedent for data privacy and cybersecurity matters and does not carve out regulatory action from the definition of a Material Adverse Effect. The standard playbook treats regulatory action arising from cross-border data transfer noncompliance as a risk that should be borne by the party controlling the relevant data operations and regulatory posture.

IV.B. Counterparty Markup Change

The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the MAE definition for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter. These carve-outs would exclude from the definition of MAE any adverse effect arising from or attributable to regulatory proceedings, investigations, consent decrees, or enforcement actions tied to the cross-border transfer of personal data and related compliance obligations.

IV.C. Transfer Impact Summary Reconciliation

The disclosure schedules directly intersect this deviation. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that are active with respect to the data transfer operations at issue. These two pending inquiries are precisely the type of regulatory action the counterparty's MAE carve-outs would exclude from the definition of an MAE.

The significance is substantial: if the MAE carve-out is accepted in the markup's form, the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 — and any adverse outcome arising from those inquiries — would be carved out of the MAE analysis. This would deprive our client of the ability to invoke an MAE closing condition or termination right based on those pending inquiries, even if they materialize into adverse regulatory outcomes. Given that the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, Schedule 3.7's disclosure confirms the real and immediate regulatory exposure these carve-outs are designed to blunt.

IV.D. Partner Instruction

The partner instruction does not grant any concession on the MAE carve-outs. The only instructed concession is the basket conversion (Deviation 1). The absence of any partner instruction authorizing acceptance of the MAE carve-outs means the markup's MAE revision remains firmly opposed under the governing analysis priorities.

IV.E. Deviation Assessment

  — MAE carve-outs for regulatory action: NOT CONCEDED; must be rejected.
    The carve-outs would exempt the very regulatory exposures disclosed in
    Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries) from the MAE definition,
    materially weakening the closing protection and termination rights that
    depend on MAE.

  Severity: HIGH
  Recommended action: Reject the added carve-outs; counterpropose MAE
  definition as set forth in the original draft, without carve-outs for
  regulatory action of the kind at issue. Reference Schedule 3.7 to make clear
  that the carve-outs would remove critical protections related to the two
  disclosed pending regulatory inquiries.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

V. DEVIATION 3 — SURVIVAL PERIOD: REDUCTION FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

V.A. Original Draft / Playbook Position

Exhibit B of the original materials sets forth the survival matrix for representations and warranties. Under the firm's standard playbook, core representations carry a survival period that aligns with the applicable statute of limitations, providing our client with adequate time to identify and pursue claims. The survival matrix is the agreed baseline for this transaction.

V.B. Counterparty Markup Change

The counterparty markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival window for the core representations. This directly contradicts Exhibit B.

V.C. Transfer Impact Summary Reconciliation

Exhibit B establishes a survival matrix. The markup's limitation-period change is inconsistent with and contradicts the survival periods set forth in Exhibit B. Because Schedule/Exhibit documents control over general statements in the base materials, the original Exhibit B survival matrix governs as the operative baseline. The counterparty's proposed survival-period reduction therefore constitutes a direct contradiction of the controlling exhibit.

V.D. Partner Instruction

Under the controlling partner instruction, the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This is the strongest possible position — a reduction in the survival period for the core representations is an unacceptable deviation that, if maintained, could terminate the deal. The partner's directive explicitly designates survival-period reduction as a walk-away matter, which elevates this issue to the highest priority for resolution.

Importantly, the latest partner message establishes that the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. Earlier messages in the thread stated the opposite priority ordering, but the latest message controls and must be followed.

V.E. Deviation Assessment

  — Survival-period reduction for core representations: WALK-AWAY ISSUE.
    Per the controlling partner instruction, any survival-period reduction is
    a walk-away issue. The counterparty's markup shortens the survival of
    the core representations, contradicting Exhibit B's survival matrix. This
    is the highest-severity deviation in the markup and must be rejected
    outright. If the counterparty does not withdraw the limitation-period
    change, the matter may reach a walk-away threshold.

  Severity: CRITICAL (walk-away)
  Recommended action: Reject the limitation-period reduction; demand the
  survival matrix per Exhibit B be restored in full. Escalate to partner if the
  counterparty holds this position, consistent with the walk-away designation.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VI. PRIORITIZED DEVIATION SUMMARY

The following table summarizes the three deviations, their controlling treatment, and recommended action, ranked by priority:

  #  Deviation                              Status          Severity / Action
  ―  ─────────────────────────────────────  ──────────────  ─────────────────────
  1  Survival-period reduction for core     Reject —       CRITICAL (walk-away)
     representations                       walk-away issue  Demand restoration of
     (contra Exhibit B)                                    Exhibit B survival matrix

  2  MAE carve-outs for regulatory action   Reject —       HIGH
     (contra Schedule 3.7                   no concession   Counterpropose original
     pending inquiries)                                   MAE definition; cite
                                                           Schedule 3.7 disclosures

  3  Indemnification cap reduction          Reject —       HIGH
     (contra Schedule 5.2                  not conceded    Counterpropose to restore
     retained liabilities)                                firm-standard cap

  —  Basket conversion: deductible       Conceded —       Per partner instruction,
     to tipping basket                   accept            no further negotiation

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VII. CONTROLLING INSTRUCTIONS AND GOVERNANCE

The partner instructions received through the deal team correspondence are the controlling authority for this analysis. Specifically:

  • The latest partner message mandates that the client will concede the basket
    conversion. This supersedes those earlier messages in the thread that stated
    the opposite priority ordering. The deliverable reflects this controlling
    instruction.

  • The client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This
    designation is absolute and unqualified, and elevates the survival-period
    deviation to critical severity.
